stories.headline: Peace along LAC: India, China hold military-level talks in Arunachal
stories.title: Peace along LAC: India, China hold military-level talks in Arunachal
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Indian and Chinese armies held high-level talks this month in the Arunachal Pradesh sector focusing on border management and addressing outstanding issues along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the Indian government said on Wednesday in the first official confirmation of the talks.

Responding to questions on Wednesday, Ministry of External Affairs official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, “India and China engage regularly through diplomatic and military mechanisms and you are well aware of those mechanisms.
A meeting of the senior military commanders was held in the eastern sector recently.
Discussions between the two sides focused on improving border management as well as addressing outstanding issues along the LAC.”
Jaiswal said such interactions are aimed at maintaining peace and tranquility in the border areas and preventing any escalation.

The Indian Express had reported on November 22 that India and China have concluded a second round of Corps Commander-level talks to resolve tensions along the frontier in Arunachal Pradesh before winter sets in fully.
The closely guarded talks, which began immediately after Diwali on November 8, continued for nearly 10 days with a short break in between.

Lt General Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Army’s III Corps (also called the Spear Corps – with its headquarters at Rangapahar near Dimapur in Nagaland) held talks with his Chinese counterpart and other officers.
An official from the MEA was also present.
This round of talks was held to set engagement rules between the two sides, avoid friction between troops on the ground, ensure open communication lines between both sides and bring down tensions.
Both sides have troops in large numbers in the area.
India and China held their first Corps Commander-level talks in the eastern sector on September 6-7 this year.

stories.headline: Why US is attacking Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat in new tariff threat
stories.title: Why US is attacking Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat in new tariff threat
stories.summary: Why US is attacking Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat in new tariff threat
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The US Trade Representative has determined that India's acts, policies and practices relating to structural excess capacity and production are "unreasonable" and burden or restrict US commerce.
It has proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods, to which New Delhi has responded by rejecting the charge.
India is expanding factories, strengthening supply chains and developing domestic industries to increase its manufacturing capacity and establish itself as a major global manufacturing hub.
Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat (Self-Reliant India) and the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes have been central to that push.
But the Donald Trump administration took a very different reading of these policies.

Washington is arguing that India's drive for self-reliance risks producing too much manufacturing capacity and output, particularly when domestic demand does not keep pace with the factories being built.
That, US officials say, can push Indian companies towards export markets, where they compete with American manufacturers.
The Trump administration has used this argument to justify imposing tariffs on India.

The US Trade Representative has determined that India's acts, policies and practices relating to structural excess capacity and production are "unreasonable" and burden or restrict US commerce under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
It also claimed that a range of India's industrial and trade practices contribute to "structural excess capacity and production" and has proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods.
The rate could be lowered to 17 per cent if the two countries reach a qualifying trade agreement.
Imagine a country builds factories capable of producing 100 units of a product when its domestic market needs only 60.

stories.title: CJI calls for greater representation to women in legal profession
stories.summary: Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant called for at least one-third women juniors in senior advocates' chambers and more women panel lawyers at the Shashi Prabha Singh Memorial Awards.

article_sentences: Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant called for at least one-third women juniors in senior advocates' chambers and more women panel lawyers at the Shashi Prabha Singh Memorial Awards.

New Delhi: Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant has called for greater representation of women in the legal profession, asking senior advocates to ensure that at least one-third of junior lawyers in their chambers are women.

Addressing the inaugural Shashi Prabha Singh Memorial Awards ceremony at the Siri Fort Sports Complex here, the CJI on Wednesday also stressed the need to appoint more women as panel lawyers to strengthen their participation and representation at the Bar.

The awards, instituted in memory of the late mother of senior advocate and former Supreme Court Bar Association president Vikas Singh, were presented to four young women advocates in recognition of their potential and contributions to litigation.
The initiative also aims to provide financial assistance to help them advance their legal careers.
The CJI underscored the imperative to create equitable opportunities for women in the legal profession.
He urged that every senior advocate engaging juniors should ensure that at least one out of every three juniors in their chambers is a woman advocate.
Lawyer Monika Dhiman received the Nyaya Prabha Ratna award, while Huma Anjum and Priyanshi Kumari were jointly honoured with the Nyaya Prabha Gaurav award.
Lawyer Kavana Rao received the Nyaya Prabha Samman.

stories.headline: Sheshnag: Kashmir’s Sacred Lake Under Threat
stories.title: Sheshnag: Kashmir’s Sacred Lake Under Threat
stories.summary: At 3,590 metres (about 11,780 feet), Sheshnag Lake is far more than a halt on the Amarnath pilgrimage. It anchors the ecology of the entire Liddar valley in south Kashmir. Set high in the upper reaches of Pahalgam in Anantnag district, this fragile alpine lake is fed by meltwater from the Kolahoi and Sheshnag glaciers. Its outflow becomes the Liddar river, which supplies clean drinking water to Pahalgam, Bijbehara, Anantnag and hundreds of villages before it joins the Jhelum. Kashmir’s orchards, paddy and tourism economy all depend on this mountain water system. Yet earthmovers, JCBs and bulldozers are now digging and widening a road along the very edge of this delicate ecosystem. Video and photographs of machines cutting into the lake’s banks have triggered sharp reactions across the Valley. Young people and trekkers have protested peacefully on Srinagar’s Shankaracharya hill, and thousands have signed online petitions. Political parties, religious leaders and environmental groups such as the Jammu and Kashmir Climate Action Group are demanding that the excavation stop immediately and that the project’s environmental clearances be made public. The Border Roads Organisation argues that widening the route is necessary to ease traffic, make the yatra smoother and strengthen safety. But the real question is whether a pilgrimage can be made convenient by gambling with the very nature that gives the journey its meaning. Science says it cannot. A recent study in Scientific Reports found that about 16.2 percent of the Baltal-Amarnath corridor falls in the highly landslide-prone category, while 68.1 percent is moderately susceptible. Researchers analysed 49 major landslides in the corridor, and 71.4 percent of them occurred in zones already rated highly susceptible. Most striking, 60 to 70 percent of the mapped slope failures lay within 50 metres of roads, tracks or other human intervention. When slopes steeper than 25 degrees are cut with heavy machinery, the rock loses its natural grip, and rain or snowmelt can then bring the hillside down. Sheshnag’s geology magnifies the danger. The lake rests on natural embankments of loose rock, soil and debris left by glaciers over thousands of years, known as moraines, along with permafrost. It is among the 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified by the Jammu and Kashmir administration, where a glacial lake outburst flood is a real threat. Excavation in its catchment can weaken those moraine dams. If debris or boulders slide into the lake, the water level can surge and breach the natural barrier. The floods from South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim and from glacial lakes in Nepal showed how quickly meddling in the high Himalaya can sweep away everything downstream. Climate data deepen the concern. Weather records for the Baltal-Amarnath region show average temperatures rising by roughly 2°C in recent decades, with a steady increase of about 0.05°C a year. Between 1994 and 2024, the valley recorded 54 extreme rainfall events, days with more than 45 millimetres of rain. The July 2022 cloudburst near the Amarnath cave, and the deluge of debris that killed pilgrims, is still fresh in public memory. Geologists, including Prof. Shakil Ahmad Romshoo, vice chancellor of the Islamic University of Science and Technology, have documented the rapid retreat of the Kolahoi glacier. Black carbon from heavy machinery and vehicles settles on snow and ice, absorbing more solar heat and speeding up melting. Ecologically, Sheshnag is an oligotrophic lake: low in nutrients and rich in dissolved oxygen. Such high-altitude lakes have very little capacity to cleanse themselves. Soil and construction debris from hill-cutting that enters the water settles as silt, reducing the lake’s depth and storage capacity and destroying aquatic life and alpine vegetation. If the lake’s water system is contaminated, the damage will fall directly on the drinking water and farming of Pahalgam and Anantnag. Millions of families with no link to the pilgrimage business would suffer. Uttarakhand’s experience is a living, bitter warning. The Kedarnath disaster and the land subsidence in Joshimath proved that the young, brittle Himalayan mountains have a limited carrying capacity. When that limit is breached in the name of development and tourism, nature restores its own balance, and humans pay the price. After those tragedies, Uttarakhand’s administration was compelled to cap pilgrim numbers in sensitive areas and restrict mechanised construction near glaciers. The Supreme Court and the National Green Tribunal have repeatedly invoked the precautionary principle, directing that any infrastructure in the high Himalaya must first undergo a transparent, independent environmental impact assessment. Before pushing Kashmir toward a Joshimath or Kedarnath of its own, policymakers must rethink their priorities. The safety and ease of pilgrims matter, but the answer does not lie in indiscriminate road widening and bulldozers on a lake’s shore. A controlled, eco-friendly model, as in the Swiss Alps, is possible: limited entry, natural protection of footpaths, relocation of temporary camps to landslide-free sites, and options such as ropeways in the most sensitive stretches. The government should halt all mechanised digging in and around Sheshnag at once, and commission a committee of independent glacier experts and ecologists to assess the whole area scientifically. A road built by hollowing out our water sources and the foundations of our mountains is not progress. It is a path to self-destruction. Pankaj Chaturvedi, Senior Journalist & Environmentalist

stories.headline: Supreme Court's Sabarimala verdict due before Christmas; Knanaya endogamy case deferred as ruling may have a bearing
stories.title: Supreme Court's Sabarimala verdict due before Christmas; Knanaya endogamy case deferred as ruling may have a bearing
stories.summary: The Supreme Court indicated that the Sabarimala reference verdict could come before the Christmas break and deferred the Knanaya Church’s endogamy case to January 2027.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: Kasaragod: The Supreme Court on Wednesday indicated that its verdict in the Sabarimala reference on women's entry into the hill shrine would be delivered before the Christmas break.

The indication came while the apex court was hearing a challenge by the Knanaya Catholic Church against a Kerala High Court judgment that struck down the Church's practice of enforcing endogamy by excluding members who marry outside the community.
The Bench deferred the Knanaya petitions, observing that the Sabarimala ruling could have a bearing on the issues involved.

A three-judge Bench of Justices B V Nagarathna, R Mahadevan and Sanjeev Sachdeva deferred the Knanaya petitions to January 5, 2027, indicating that they would be considered after the nine-judge Constitution Bench delivers its verdict in the Sabarimala reference.

Justice B V Nagarathna said that the Sabarimala verdict was likely to be delivered before the Supreme Court closes for its Christmas vacation on December 18, Adv Sai Shashank, who represents the reformist group in the Knanaya case, told Onmanorama.
The nine-judge Bench had reserved its judgment on May 14 after 16 days of hearings.
The Sabarimala reference, however, goes beyond the question of women’s entry into the hill shrine.
Several other disputes involving religious practices and the rights of religious denominations have been tagged with the reference for consideration by the larger Bench, said Adv Shashank.

These include challenges concerning the entry of Muslim women into mosques and dargahs, the exclusion of Parsi women from fire temples after marrying outside the community, and the practice of female genital mutilation among the Dawoodi Bohra community.
The reference also encompasses the Dawoodi Bohra community’s power to excommunicate members, he said.

The larger Bench is examining constitutional questions on the scope of religious freedom under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution, the autonomy of religious denominations, the limits of judicial scrutiny of religious practices and the relationship between individual rights and denominational rights.

The Knanaya dispute raises a closely related question: whether a religious community can invoke its right to manage its own affairs to enforce endogamy, or whether an individual’s right to choose a spouse takes precedence.

stories.headline: US proposes 25 per cent tariffs on India; 17 per cent if trade deal clinched
stories.title: US proposes 25 per cent tariffs on India; 17 per cent if trade deal clinched
stories.summary: Washington, Nov 25: The US on Wednesday proposed 25 per cent tariffs on Indian goods in the absence of a trade deal, citing excess industrial capacity, sustained market access barriers and inadequate labour protection that harm American companies. The US Trade Representative (USTR) said the tariffs on India would amount to 17 per cent if it agrees to a trade deal with America. The fresh tariff proposal follows Section 301 investigations launched by the USTR in March targeting 16 economic jurisdictions. The USTR proposed tariffs of up to 20 per cent to 35 per cent on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place. The EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland face 15 per cent tariff rates, inclusive of standard import duties. Vietnam would face tariffs of 20 per cent if the trade deal is finalised. “For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base,” said USTR Jamieson Greer. “India generates trade surpluses in sectors such as pharmaceuticals, steel, and ICT goods, revealing dependencies on Indian manufacturing in certain key sectors,” the USTR said in its report on ‘India's Acts, Policies, and Practices Relating to Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors’. These new tariffs would not be added to existing ones aimed at combating forced labour or certain sector-specific tariffs, a senior US official said. The USTR has decided to schedule public hearings on its proposals on January 25 and sought written comments from interested persons by January 5. The Office of the USTR has been analysing for several months whether 16 jurisdictions have policies that favour surplus production, a practice that drives down prices and harms US industry. The investigation began last March, after the Supreme Court overturned the indiscriminate trade levies imposed by the Trump administration invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). After that reversal, the USTR opened two investigations based on Article 301: one directed at 60 jurisdictions (about a hundred countries) for violating export regulations on forced labour; and the other against 16 jurisdictions for promoting surplus production. India and the US are negotiating an interim bilateral trade agreement after the framework they had finalised in February went back to the discussion board with the Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA tariffs imposed last year. India is seeking lower tariffs for its goods in the US market than its competitors such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia. “USTR is applying to India a diagnosis built for a very different economy. India consumes most of what it produces and buys more goods from the world than it sells, so it is not exporting a domestic glut,” said Abhik Sengupta, a Task Force Observer on the Committee on Strategic Trade and Market Access, Helsinki Geoeconomics Society. Sengupta said India’s reliance on Chinese inputs points to gaps in its industrial base, not a surplus. “Penalising India for closing those gaps risks pushing supply chains back toward the very economies Washington is most concerned about,” he said.

These new tariffs would not be added to existing ones aimed at combating forced labour or certain sector-specific tariffs, a senior US official said.
The USTR has decided to schedule public hearings on its proposals on January 25 and sought written comments from interested persons by January 5.
The Office of the USTR has been analysing for several months whether 16 jurisdictions have policies that favour surplus production, a practice that drives down prices and harms US industry.

The investigation began last March, after the Supreme Court overturned the indiscriminate trade levies imposed by the Trump administration invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).

After that reversal, the USTR opened two investigations based on Article 301: one directed at 60 jurisdictions (about a hundred countries) for violating export regulations on forced labour; and the other against 16 jurisdictions for promoting surplus production.

India and the US are negotiating an interim bilateral trade agreement after the framework they had finalised in February went back to the discussion board with the Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA tariffs imposed last year.
India is seeking lower tariffs for its goods in the US market than its competitors such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia.
“USTR is applying to India a diagnosis built for a very different economy.

India consumes most of what it produces and buys more goods from the world than it sells, so it is not exporting a domestic glut,” said Abhik Sengupta, a Task Force Observer on the Committee on Strategic Trade and Market Access, Helsinki Geoeconomics Society.
Sengupta said India’s reliance on Chinese inputs points to gaps in its industrial base, not a surplus.
“Penalising India for closing those gaps risks pushing supply chains back toward the very economies Washington is most concerned about,” he said.

stories.headline: A commitment to strengthen our Constitution
stories.title: A commitment to strengthen our Constitution
stories.summary: On 26th November 1949, the Constituent Assembly adopted our Constitution. Today, we remember Dr. Rajendra Prasad, Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar and every member of the Constituent Assembly. Their greatness lay in drawing extensively from the rich traditions and civilisational wisdom of Bharat while framing a modern Constitution. For a nation as diverse as Bharat, with its numerous faiths, languages, customs and schools of thought, it is important that the Constitution have a resonance far beyond the precincts of Parliament and the courts. Our endeavour has been to deepen its connect with the collective consciousness of our people, especially our youth and strengthen the spirit of unity essential to India’s bright future. That is why over a decade ago, our Government decided to mark 26th November as Constitution Day. For crores of Indians, including me, the Constitution of India is an inseparable part of our life journeys. Whenever I look back at my childhood, the humble circumstances in which I grew up, the struggles that were a part of everyday life, I am filled with an overwhelming sense of gratitude towards our Constitution. That a child born into a family of modest means, with no privileges or advantages of birth, could one day be entrusted with the responsibility of serving the world’s largest democracy speaks volumes about how extraordinary our Constitution is. It is due to our Constitution that circumstances of one’s birth no longer determine the limits of one’s future. In our own humble way, we have sought to repay this debt of gratitude by strengthening our Constitution. The distinguished constitutional scholar Granville Austin described our Constitution as “ first and foremost a social document.” The quest for social and economic justice runs through the very fabric of our Constitution. Thus, what can be more satisfying than working towards the realisation of this cherished vision of the makers of our Constitution? A recent World Bank report highlights that nearly 50 crore Indians have moved out of poverty. Breaking free from generations of deprivation, crores of parents can now dream of a better future for their children. When PM Awas Yojana ensures a family moves from a thatched roof to a pucca home, the constitutional promise of dignity acquires meaning. When Ujjwala Yojana frees a mother from the hardships of a smoke-filled kitchen, we advance the ideals of equality and well-being. When Ayushman Bharat enables a poor family to access quality healthcare without the fear of debt, social justice becomes a lived reality. When MUDRA and PM-SVANidhi provide collateral-free credit to small entrepreneurs and street vendors, economic justice finds expression. When digital technology and platforms like UPI transcend all divides and place opportunities once available to a privileged few within the reach of every citizen, we advance the constitutional ideal of inclusivity. There are many more manifestations of this constitutional vision. The list of amendments we brought can be viewed through the same prism. The 101st Amendment ushered in GST, a long-awaited reform. The 102nd Amendment granted constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes, fulfilling a long-standing dream of the marginalised sections of society. The 103rd Amendment received broad social acceptance. By providing reservation to Economically Weaker Sections, it addressed the long-overlooked aspirations of economically disadvantaged families from communities outside the existing reservation framework. For the first time since 1950, an updated version of our Constitution is now available in all 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule. This has brought our Constitution closer to the people. Even after our Constitution came into force in 1950, we continued to be governed by the colonial penal code dating back to the 1860s. With the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, we have sought to bring about a fundamental shift in our criminal justice system, moving from the colonial emphasis on punishment (Dand) to a citizen-centric pursuit of justice (Nyay). Over the past decade, we have laid special emphasis on Kartavya, or the duties of a citizen. Our civilisation has always emphasised the responsibilities that accompany every role in society. The spirit of Kartavya has found expression in several mass movements, from Swachh Bharat to water conservation and environmental protection. However, there is another reality that I feel compelled to share. There have been occasions in our history when those entrusted with upholding the Constitution chose to weaken it. Ironically, they are the same people who had the opportunity to govern India for five decades. This year marks 75 years since the First Amendment of 1951, when a government that was not popularly elected used its majority in the Provisional Parliament to restrict fundamental freedoms. Its timing, barely months before India’s first general election, proves that it was intended to influence the electoral process and stifle public opposition. It is also 50 years since the 42nd Amendment at the height of the Emergency. This curtailed judicial review and fundamentally altered the balance of institutional powers. I would also urge youngsters to study the 38th and 39th Amendments to know what a power-hungry and anti-constitutional leadership can do. The repeated misuse of Article 356 to dismiss elected state governments presents another troubling chapter. One party has the dubious record of imposing Article 356 almost a hundred times and one former Prime Minister has scored a half-century in this field. The makers of our Constitution had hoped that it would be implemented in letter and spirit across India. But, for over 70 years, Articles 370 and 35A did not allow the full Constitution to be implemented in Jammu and Kashmir, thus trampling over the rights of SC, ST, OBC communities and women. It was only in 2019 that this historical wrong was corrected. For decades, in several parts of India, particularly in tribal areas, Naxalites used the might of the gun to deny the poorest people the rights guaranteed to them by our Constitution. The successful elimination of Naxalism this year is particularly heartwarming because it has ensured that the poorest of the poor can finally exercise their constitutional rights without fear. Now, we are left only with ‘Dimagi Naxals’, far removed from the realities of our times but persistent in their efforts to derail our growth trajectory. It is most appalling that the biggest party in the Opposition wants to reduce OBC reservation and bring Muslim reservations, something the makers of our Constitution, notably Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar, were totally against. The journey of our Constitution would be incomplete without recognising the remarkable women who helped shape it. But what happened earlier this year should fill our hearts with shame. A legislation aimed at giving women adequate representation in legislative bodies was disallowed from being passed by the one Opposition party, once again showing its disdain for constitutional values. I assure the Nari Shakti of India that no force can prevent us from ensuring that justice is done to them. Our constitutional democracy has a clearly defined role for the Opposition. Sadly, the leading Opposition party seems to have become more of an Avrodh Paksh (obstructionist) than a Virodh Paksh (opposition). They should know that disrupting democratic processes is no substitute for discharging constitutional responsibilities. Today, India stands at a defining moment. As we work towards Viksit Bharat by 2047, two simple yet powerful principles can guide our collective endeavours: India First in our thinking and Kartavya (Duties) in our actions. With these as our guiding principles and the Constitution as our source of strength, we can secure a bright future for generations to come. Shri Narendra Modi, Honourable Prime Minister of India
